newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Tata upbeat on SIA airline tieup.
newsitem.headline: India's Tata upbeat on SIA airline tieup.

text.p: India's Tata group said on Wednesday it was hopeful the cabinet would approve a proposed $600-million airline venture with Singapore Airlines Ltd.

Tata officials, in their first public statement on the two-year-old proposal which has divided the Indian cabinet, told a news conference that group chairman Ratan Tata met Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim last week to present his case.
The proposal to create a new domestic airline has drawn criticism from Ibrahim and strong support from Industry Minister Murasoli Maran.
"We have always remained optimistic. We have waited for two years," Sujit Gupta, director of Tata Industries Ltd, said. He described the Tata-Ibrahim meeting as "good".
The airline proposal has become a litmus test for foreign investors and stock markets assessing India's economic reforms.

Last month, India approved a new aviation policy that permits foreign investors to hold up to 40 percent stakes in domestic airlines. But the policy does not allow foreign airlines directly to hold stakes.

The Tata group proposes holding 40 percent of the planned Tata Airline with an equal stake for Singapore Airlines, which would offer technical assistance. Indian institutional investors would hold the remaining 20 percent.
"The ownership of the airline will be in the hands of Indians," said S. Ramakrishnan, vice president (projects) of Tata Industries.
The Tatas said they planned to operate only 19 aircraft by 2002, while India estimated it needed 107 aircraft including 78 new planes and 29 replacements by then.
"We do not see ourselves as a threat to Indian Airlines," Gupta said, adding the state-run Indian Airlines already had 57 aircraft on its fleet.

Ramakrishnan said the Tatas courted Singapore Airlines in order to achieve its standards in safety, service, management and training. "Equity participation along with expertise is the most ideal form," he said.

Officials said the doors were not yet closed for Singapore Airlines because the cabinet had not yet spelled out a specific policy on foreign airline stakes. News reports have said the cabinet was likely to consider the proposal again this month.
"During discussions (in the cabinet), it was felt that the Civil Aviation Ministry could look at it once again," Ibrahim recently told the Business Standard newspaper.
In December, the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), which falls under the Industry Ministry, recommended the project for approval by the cabinet.
Ibrahim has said New Delhi could not allow Singapore Airlines to take a stake in an Indian airline because Singapore does not allow more than five percent foreign stakes in its domestic airlines.
The Tata group issued a statement giving examples of domestic airlines elsewhere in the world which allow foreign airlines to hold stakes.

It said the proposed Tata Airline would comply with Indian policy requirements that make it mandatory for airlines to fly on some routes that are not financially attractive to provide broad-based customer service.
